subject: Painting and Decorating
practicalPaper: Paper 3 (Decorative Painting) is a 3-hour practical for 100 marks: candidates attempt one of two alternative tasks whose requirements are released at least two weeks before, and execute the work under WAEC supervision in poster or acrylic colours. Marks reward interpretation of the brief, composition, use of colour, technique, craftsmanship and finish.

practicals.title: Applying the elements and principles of design
practicals.aim: To create small compositions that demonstrate the elements (line, shape, colour, texture, tone, space) and principles (balance, rhythm, emphasis, unity, proportion, contrast) of design.
safety: Wash hands after painting; do not eat in the studio.
Keep the floor dry to avoid slipping.
procedure: Divide the sheet into six 10 × 12 cm panels.
In each panel, design an abstract arrangement emphasising one principle (e.g. symmetrical balance, rhythm by repetition).
Use the elements deliberately: varied lines, shapes and textures.
Lay in flat colour neatly.
Label each panel with the principle shown.
Write a short note explaining how each design achieves its effect.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each panel clearly communicates its principle; colour application is even with clean edges.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Layout: A3 paper is 420 × 297 mm. Six panels of 120 × 100 mm in a 3 × 2 grid occupy 360 × 200 mm, leaving (420 − 360)/2 = 30 mm side margins and (297 − 200)/2 = 48.5 mm top and bottom margins.
precautions: Use masking tape for crisp edges.
Allow each colour to dry before painting next to it.
commonMistakes: Mixing several principles so none is clear.
examTips: Name and define the elements and principles in theory answers.
Neat, well-planned layouts earn craftsmanship marks.

practicals.title: Mixing a colour wheel
practicals.aim: To mix secondary and tertiary colours from the three primaries and paint a 12-part colour wheel.
materials: Poster colours: red, yellow, blue, white, black
safety: Avoid swallowing paint; keep brushes out of mouths.
procedure: Draw a circle of 8 cm radius and divide it into 12 equal sectors (30° each).
Paint red, yellow and blue in sectors 4 apart (every 120°).
Mix equal amounts of neighbouring primaries to get orange, green and violet; paint them halfway between.
Mix each primary with its neighbouring secondary for the six tertiaries (e.g. yellow-orange).
Label every sector.
Mark complementary pairs with connecting lines.
practicals.expectedObservations: A smooth progression of hues around the wheel; complementary colours lie directly opposite each other.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 12 sectors × 30° = 360°. Primaries 120° apart; secondaries midway (60° from each primary); tertiaries at the 30° positions between them. Complementary pairs are 180° apart (6 sectors), e.g. red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet.
precautions: Clean the brush between colours.
Mix enough of each colour to finish its sector.
commonMistakes: Placing secondary colours next to the wrong primaries.
examTips: Define hue, tone (value) and intensity (chroma).
Draw the wheel neatly; labels earn marks.

practicals.title: Painting colour schemes and tonal scales
practicals.aim: To paint the same simple design in monochrome, analogous and complementary colour schemes and to produce a tonal (value) scale.
safety: Keep water pots stable to avoid spills on the work.
procedure: Paint a 7-step tonal scale of one hue by adding increasing amounts of white (tints) and black (shades).
Trace the same motif three times.
Paint the first using only tints and shades of one hue (monochrome).
Paint the second with three or four neighbouring hues (analogous).
Paint the third using a pair of complementary hues.
Compare the mood and contrast of the three versions.
practicals.expectedObservations: Monochrome looks calm and unified; analogous is harmonious; complementary gives strong contrast and vibrancy.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tonal scale proportions (by brush-loads): step 1 pure hue; tints 1:1, 1:2, 1:3 hue to white; shades 4:1, 3:1, 2:1 hue to black. Seven steps in a 210 mm strip gives 210/7 = 30 mm per step.
precautions: Add black very gradually; it is very strong.
Mix enough paint for each area.
commonMistakes: Using unrelated hues in an analogous scheme.
examTips: Define each colour scheme with examples.
Explain the emotional effect of warm and cool colours.

practicals.title: Improvising colours from local sources
practicals.aim: To prepare paints from local materials such as camwood, laterite, charcoal, chalk/kaolin and indigo, and test them on paper and wall samples.
apparatus: Mortar and pestle or grinding stone
materials: Camwood (osun), laterite, charcoal, kaolin (white clay), indigo leaves or dye
Binder: gum arabic, egg yolk or PVA
safety: Wear a dust mask when grinding pigments.
Some plant dyes stain skin; wear gloves.
procedure: Dry and grind each material into a fine powder.
Sieve to remove coarse particles.
Mix the powder with water and binder to a creamy paint.
Test each colour on paper and a plastered sample.
Record colour, covering power and fastness after drying and rubbing.
Paint a small motif using only local colours.
practicals.expectedObservations: Camwood gives reddish-brown, laterite earth red/ochre, charcoal black, kaolin white and indigo blue. Adequate binder stops the colour rubbing off.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Binder ratio test: 2 parts pigment to 1 part binder (by spoon) rubbed off; 3 parts pigment to 2 parts binder held well. For 50 g pigment at the better ratio (3:2), use about 50 × 2/3 ≈ 33 g of binder.
precautions: Grind finely for smooth paint.
Label each container.
commonMistakes: Too little binder (powdery) or too much (glossy, cracking).
examTips: Name local colour sources and their colours.
Explain the role of a binder.

practicals.title: Still life painting from observation
practicals.topic: Types and Functions of Pictorial Painting
practicals.aim: To compose and paint a still life group of local objects from direct observation, showing form, light and shade.
materials: Local objects: calabash, clay pot, yam, fruits, cloth drape
safety: Arrange objects securely so they do not fall.
procedure: Arrange 3–5 objects with a drape and a single light source.
Use the viewfinder to choose the composition.
Sketch lightly, checking proportions by sight-size measuring with the pencil.
Block in large areas of colour and the background.
Model forms with light, mid and dark tones; add cast shadows.
Add details and highlights last.
Sign and title the work.
practicals.expectedObservations: Objects appear solid and correctly proportioned with consistent light direction.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Sight-size measuring: if the pot measures 3 pencil units high and the calabash 2 units, the calabash should be drawn two-thirds the height of the pot; a pot drawn 15 cm high means a calabash 15 × 2/3 = 10 cm high.
precautions: Keep your viewing position fixed.
Work from general to particular.
examTips: Distinguish still life, nature (landscape) and figure painting.
Explain observatory versus imaginative composition.

practicals.title: Pictorial techniques: wet, dry, glazing and impasto
practicals.aim: To produce sample panels showing wet-on-wet, dry brush, glazing and impasto techniques, and to describe fresco and tempera.
safety: Wash palette knives carefully; edges can cut.
procedure: Wet: wet the paper and drop in colour; observe soft blending.
Dry: drag a nearly dry stiff brush over textured paper to create broken texture.
Glazing: paint a dry underlayer, then apply thin transparent layers to modify the colour.
Impasto: apply thick paint with a palette knife to create raised texture.
Tempera: mix pigment with egg yolk and paint small hatched strokes.
Label each sample and note uses.
practicals.expectedObservations: Wet technique gives soft edges; dry brush gives broken texture; glazes give luminous depth; impasto gives raised, textured surfaces.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Glaze mixture: about 1 part colour to 4 parts acrylic medium gives a transparent glaze — 5 mL colour to 20 mL medium makes 25 mL of glaze, which is 5/25 = 20% colour.
precautions: Let glazes dry fully before the next layer.
sourcesOfError: Fast drying of acrylic in hot weather.
examTips: Describe each technique in one or two sentences with its effect.
Fresco is painted on wet lime plaster; tempera uses egg as binder.

practicals.title: Decorative finishes: flat painting, rag rolling and combing
practicals.aim: To prepare sample boards with flat painting, rag rolling, scumbling/combing and sponging effects for interior decoration.
safety: Ventilate when using solvent-based glazes.
Dispose of oily rags flat to dry (fire risk).
procedure: Sand and prime the boards.
Apply two flat base coats with roller or brush; allow to dry.
Rag rolling: apply glaze, then roll a twisted rag over it to lift a random pattern.
Combing: drag a comb through wet glaze in straight or wavy lines.
Sponging: dab glaze on with a sponge.
Compare effects and suggest suitable rooms for each.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each method gives a distinct texture: rag rolling looks like crushed fabric, combing gives linear patterns, sponging a mottled look.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Wall area for a 4 m × 3.5 m room, 3 m high: perimeter = 2 × (4 + 3.5) = 15 m; area = 15 × 3 = 45 m², minus a door (2 m²) and window (1.5 m²) = 41.5 m². Two coats at 10 m² per litre need 41.5 × 2/10 = 8.3 L of emulsion.
precautions: Work in manageable sections while glaze is wet.
Keep a wet edge to avoid lap marks.
sourcesOfError: Glaze drying too fast in heat.
examTips: Describe each decorative technique and where it is used.
Show area and paint quantity calculation.

practicals.title: Designing a mosaic panel
practicals.aim: To design and make a small mosaic panel using locally available tesserae.
materials: Tesserae: broken tiles, coloured paper squares, seeds, bottle caps, glass pieces
safety: Wear goggles and gloves when cutting tiles or glass.
Sweep up sharp fragments.
procedure: Draw a bold design with simple shapes on paper and transfer it to the board.
Sort tesserae by colour.
Glue tesserae along outlines first (andamento), leaving small even gaps.
Fill background areas.
For tile mosaics, grout the gaps and wipe clean.
Clean and seal the panel.
practicals.expectedObservations: The design reads clearly from a distance; gaps are even and pieces lie flat.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Panel 30 × 30 cm = 900 cm². With 1.5 cm square tesserae plus about 0.2 cm gaps, each piece covers about 1.7 × 1.7 = 2.89 cm², so roughly 900/2.89 ≈ 311 pieces are needed.
precautions: Keep gaps uniform.
Use strong adhesive.
commonMistakes: Too much detail for the size of the tesserae.
examTips: Define mosaic and mural; give examples in public buildings.
Show estimation of materials.

practicals.title: Enlarging a design for a wall mural
practicals.aim: To design a wall decoration using traditional or modern motifs and enlarge it accurately to wall size by the grid method.
safety: Use a stable trestle; do not over-reach on ladders.
Cover floors and furniture.
procedure: Research traditional motifs (e.g. uli, nsibidi, adire patterns) or modern designs.
Produce a coloured design to scale.
Draw a grid over the design.
Mark a proportionally larger grid on the wall with chalk line and level.
Transfer the design square by square.
Paint background areas first, then motifs and details.
Protect with a clear coat if exterior.
practicals.expectedObservations: The wall image keeps the proportions of the design; motifs are crisp and evenly coloured.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Design 30 × 20 cm enlarged to 1.5 × 1.0 m: scale factor = 150/30 = 5. A 2 cm grid on the design becomes a 10 cm grid on the wall: 15 squares across × 10 squares down.
precautions: Check the grid is level and square before drawing.
Keep design proportions identical.
commonMistakes: Using different scale factors horizontally and vertically.
examTips: Compare traditional and modern wall decoration and materials.
State functions of wall decoration (beauty, identity, communication).

practicals.title: Designing motifs for body decoration
practicals.aim: To study traditional and modern body decoration motifs and design a set of motifs on paper suitable for henna, uli or face painting.
materials: Henna paste or brown/black ink (for paper samples)
Paper cut-outs of hands and faces
safety: Do not apply chemical "black henna" (PPD) to skin; it can cause severe allergic reactions.
Patch-test any natural material before skin use, with consent.
procedure: Identify motifs from local traditions (uli, laali/henna, tribal marks as historical study, modern face painting).
Note materials: camwood, uli juice, henna, kohl, modern face paints.
Design a border, central and filler motif.
Arrange them on paper hand and face templates.
Render in ink or henna on paper.
Write the meaning or function of each motif.
practicals.expectedObservations: Designs follow the shape of the body part, using symmetry and rhythm, and reflect cultural meaning.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Repetition for a bracelet band: a wrist of 16 cm circumference with a 2 cm repeating motif needs 16/2 = 8 repeats.
precautions: Use only safe materials for skin work.
examTips: State differences between traditional and modern body decoration.
List materials and functions (beauty, identity, ceremonies).

practicals.title: One- and two-point perspective drawing
practicals.aim: To draw a street or room scene in linear perspective and demonstrate aerial (atmospheric) perspective in colour.
safety: Normal studio safety.
procedure: Draw the horizon line at eye level.
One-point: place a vanishing point and draw a road or corridor with all receding lines meeting there.
Add buildings, poles and figures that diminish in size with distance.
Two-point: draw a building corner with two vanishing points on the horizon.
Paint a landscape where distant hills become paler and bluer (aerial perspective).
Label horizon line and vanishing points.
practicals.expectedObservations: Objects of equal size appear smaller as they recede; distant colours are lighter, cooler and less detailed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Equal-height poles: a pole 6 cm tall at the front and half-way to the vanishing point appears about 3 cm tall; the tops of all poles lie on a line drawn from the first pole top to the vanishing point.
precautions: Keep the vanishing points on the horizon line.
Use a ruler for converging lines.
sourcesOfError: Vanishing points too close, distorting shapes.
commonMistakes: Receding lines not meeting at one point.
examTips: Define linear and aerial perspective and state their importance in pictorial composition.

practicals.title: Costing a painting commission
practicals.aim: To prepare a cost and price estimate for a painting or decorative job based on size, materials, time, location and quality.
materials: Job brief (e.g. mural 3 m × 2 m in a school hall)
safety: When measuring on site, use stable ladders and work in pairs.
procedure: Measure the work area.
List materials and quantities with prices.
Estimate hours of labour and set an hourly rate.
Add overheads (transport, equipment hire) for the location.
Add a profit margin for quality and reputation.
Present a neat quotation.
practicals.expectedObservations: A clear quotation that the client can understand and that covers all costs.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mural 3 m × 2 m = 6 m². Materials ₦40 000; labour 30 h × ₦1 500 = ₦45 000; transport and scaffold ₦15 000. Cost = 40 000 + 45 000 + 15 000 = ₦100 000. With 30% profit, price = ₦130 000, i.e. about ₦21 667 per m².
precautions: Use current market prices.
Include contingency for waste.
examTips: List factors affecting price: location, size, materials, time, quantity, quality.
Show every step of the calculation.

practicals.title: Planning and mounting an exhibition
practicals.aim: To plan, budget, hang and publicise a small class exhibition of paintings.
apparatus: Hammer and picture hooks or display boards
safety: Secure heavy frames properly; keep walkways clear.
Use stable ladders when hanging.
procedure: Set a theme, date and venue; form committees (publicity, hanging, finance).
Prepare a budget and seek funding (school, sponsors, gate fees).
Mount and label works (title, artist, medium, size, price).
Plan the hanging layout to scale; hang at eye level, evenly spaced.
Publicise with posters and social media.
Run the exhibition and record sales and visitors.
Evaluate.
practicals.expectedObservations: Works are level and evenly spaced at a consistent centre height; visitors move easily.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Wall 8 m long for 6 works each 0.6 m wide: total width 3.6 m; space left 8 − 3.6 = 4.4 m divided into 7 equal gaps (including both ends) = 0.63 m per gap. Hang with picture centres at about 1.5 m above the floor.
precautions: Check each picture with a spirit level.
examTips: Describe planning stages and sources of funding.
Include a budget table.
